Dear Hiring Manager,

I am applying for the Staff Engineer role. For the past six years I have been a backend engineer, most of that time on payments systems, and I want to bring that depth to a UK fintech where reliability and correctness matter as much as speed.

Payments work has taught me to treat money movement as a set of guarantees: idempotent request handling, reconciliation against external schemes and banks, and designing for partial failure so that a retry never becomes a double charge. I have led design work on services that process high volumes of transactions, and I have spent a lot of time with the people on the other side of those systems, including ops, support, and finance, because a payments bug is rarely only an engineering problem.

At staff level, I want to focus on the things that make a platform hold up over time: clear service boundaries, observability that tells you what happened to a payment rather than just that something failed, and migration plans that let teams change core flows without freezing the roadmap. I have mentored engineers through design reviews and have worked to make those reviews a shared habit rather than a gate.

I would welcome the chance to talk about how my experience maps to your current challenges. Thank you for considering my application.

Yours sincerely,

[Your name]

Hey, thanks for sending the design doc over. The problem statement is clear, and that's a real strength. A reader can tell within a paragraph what's broken and why it matters, so keep doing that.

Two things to work on before this is ready for review.

**The alternatives section is missing.** This is the part reviewers will look for first. Even if you think your approach is obviously right, list the other options you considered, including the do-nothing option, and say why you didn't pick each one. You don't need many. Two or three real alternatives with a sentence or two each is plenty. It also protects you: when someone asks "did you think about X?" and the answer is already in the doc, the review moves on quickly.

**The rollout plan needs dates.** Right now it says things like "first we'll ship to a small group, then expand." Put calendar dates on each step, even rough ones, and say who owns each step and what would make you pause or roll back. A plan with dates lets people tell you whether the timeline works for them. A plan without dates leaves everyone guessing.

If it helps, send me a revised draft when you have one and I'll read through it. Nice work getting the first one this far.

Pick two or three realistic options, including doing nothing, and for each one write a short paragraph on what it costs, what it fixes, and where it falls short. Then say which one you picked and why. Even if the choice feels obvious to you, writing out the rejected options makes the doc much easier to approve.

The rollout plan needs dates. "Phase 1, then phase 2" tells people the order but not the timing, so nobody can plan around it. Put a calendar date on each phase, name the person who owns it, and say what has to be true before the next phase starts. If a date is a guess, say so and say what would move it. A plan with a rough date is more useful than one with none.

Once those two sections are in, send it back and I'll read it again.

Here's feedback you can adapt for your colleague:

---

Thanks for sending over your first design doc. I can tell you put real thought into it, and a lot of this is already in good shape.

**What's working: the problem statement**

The problem statement is clear. It says what's broken, who it affects, and why it matters now, without jumping to a solution. That's the hardest part of a design doc, and you got it right. Keep writing problem statements this way.

**Needs work: the alternatives section is missing**

A design doc is mainly a record of a decision, and the alternatives section is where a reviewer checks that you considered other options. Without it, reviewers have to guess whether you looked at anything besides your proposal, and they'll often ask questions you've already answered.

For each alternative you considered, including "do nothing," try to cover:
- A one-sentence description
- The main advantages and disadvantages
- Why you didn't choose it

Even options you rejected quickly are worth a line. If the reason is "too much work for the benefit," say that. It shows the decision was deliberate. If you're unsure what counts as an alternative, ask yourself, "What would a reasonable engineer on the team propose instead?" and write that down.

**Needs work: the rollout plan needs dates**

The rollout plan describes the right phases, but without dates it's hard for anyone to plan around the work or hold it accountable. For each phase, add:
- A target start and end date (or a week number if exact dates aren't set yet)
- The owner or team responsible
- The exit criteria, meaning how you'll know the phase succeeded before moving on

If the dates depend on something outside your control, like another team's release, note that dependency explicitly. Reviewers will then know which dates are firm and which are estimates.

**Next steps**

1. Add an alternatives section, even a rough one. Ask one teammate who knows the space to help you fill gaps.
2. Add dates and owners to the rollout plan. Estimates are fine. Mark them as estimates.
3. Send the revised draft to me before it goes to the wider review.

Nice work on the first draft. The structure is solid, and these additions will make it much easier for reviewers to say yes.
